source_refs.note: Book p. 222: 12.2 Limits of Important Functions, own text before 12.2.1 (substitution gives 0/0; simplify by making factors and cancelling common factors).

blocks.text: If by substituting the number that \(x\) approaches into the function, we get \(\left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\), then we evaluate the limits as follows:
We simplify the given function by using the algebraic technique of making factors (if possible) and cancel the common factors. The method is explained in the following important limits.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
In 12.1 we found most limits by simply substituting the value of \(x\). This section is about the cases where substitution gives \(\frac{0}{0}\).
\(\frac{0}{0}\) is not a number and it is not the answer. It is called an indeterminate form: it only tells us that the function, in its present shape, cannot be evaluated at that point. The limit may still exist and may be any number. We must first change the shape of the function by algebra, and then substitute.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
An example of our own shows the whole method. Find \(\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}\).
Substituting \(x = 2\) gives \(\frac{4-4}{2-2} = \frac{0}{0}\), so we factorize:
\[\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2} = \dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}\]
\[= x + 2 \quad (x \ne 2)\]
\[\lim_{x\to 2}\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2} = 2 + 2 = 4\]
Why may we cancel \(x - 2\)? "\(x \to 2\)" means \(x\) comes very close to 2 but is never equal to 2 (12.1.3). So \(x - 2 \ne 0\), and dividing by it is allowed.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The common factor that makes \(\frac{0}{0}\) is always the factor that becomes zero at the point. If \(x \to a\) gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), look for the factor \((x - a)\) in both the numerator and the denominator.
The next sub-sections use three tools to remove it:
1. Factorization, e.g. \(x^{n} - a^{n} = (x-a)(\dots)\) (12.2.1).
2. Rationalization, when square roots are present (12.2.2).
3. For limits at infinity (\(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) type), dividing by the highest power of \(x\) in the denominator (12.2.3 to 12.2.5).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In the exam, first show the substitution and write "\(\frac{0}{0}\) form". This one line shows the examiner why you are factorizing, and it earns credit for the method.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Always try substitution first. If it gives a number, that number is the limit.
2. If it gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), the limit is not yet known: simplify the function first.
3. Factorize, cancel the common factor (it is non-zero because \(x \ne a\)), then substitute.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\frac{0}{0} = 0\) or \(\frac{0}{0} = 1\) and stopping. \(\frac{0}{0}\) has no value; it is a signal to simplify.
2. Cancelling a factor that is not common to both the numerator and the denominator.
3. Dropping the word "Lim" in the middle lines before substituting. Keep \(\lim_{x\to a}\) in every line until you actually put \(x = a\).
